name: Doe
lede: Doe is a light, warm tan from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, named for the female deer, and one of the most common colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: The color of a deer's coat
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930), as cited by NBS Circular 553 (1955), records Doe on plate 13, row B, column 6, first appearing in print around 1902 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system reads the swatch as "light brown," its block 57 [1]. The name is a plain animal reference, the female deer's tan coat, and none of the 29 books in our concordance adds more to that [2].

In LCH terms it measures lightness 55, chroma 29, hue 72 degrees, Munsell 9.0YR 5.4/4.5 [1]. Its closest match in the library is [[cork]], about 2.8 CIEDE2000 units away, with [[mocha]] tied at the same distance [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A match within six CIEDE2000 units covering at least five percent of the canvas turns up in 4,115 of our 23,781 archive paintings, about 17.3 percent, one of the most common colors we track [4]. It is strongest in the 1300s, at 2.4 times the overall rate, and carried by painters across eras: Peter Paul Rubens in twenty-seven of his fifty-five paintings here, Maarten van Heemskerck in eight of twelve [4]. It most often plays a highlight, in 65 percent of its appearances, and is especially common in Japanese and Korean paintings in the archive [4].

The earliest dated match is the *Funerary Papyrus of Tayuhenutmut*, from about 1069 BC, nearly three thousand years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930; early centuries are thin in the archive, so this is a floor, not a first, and a photograph of an aged canvas is a screen color, not a pigment test [4].
